## Any shape you want {transition="slide-in none-out"}

![](img/play_doh-1.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.caption}
Four separate colors, until you start building
:::

::: {.notes}
**Complication — 35 s**

On the box there is a parrot. It looks fantastic. I tried — mine did not look like
the parrot. I was more of a lego kid.

Any shape you want, as long as you can make it. Every shape by hand, every time,
from nothing.

That is what infinite malleability costs you: nothing you make is reusable.
Tailor-made pieces don't just fit together, so the logic you would want to carry
over can't be separated from the app it grew inside.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
How do you make the next app cheaper than this one?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Question + hook — 20 s**

So: how do you make the next app cheaper than this one?

**By taking things away.** By adding restrictions.

The stud is the trade: the thing that limits what shapes you can build is the same
thing that lets the pieces connect.

You are building an approximation of the perfect shape. When that's acceptable, you
get a material that is far easier to wield.

*Shot brief — two different models from obviously shared brick types. Loose bricks
say modular; two models say reused, which is the actual claim.*

*Memorable line — one breath, quotable enough to survive to the hallway. Try it
with and without the words on screen.*
:::

## A block {transition="slide-in none-out"}

![](img/lego-2.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.caption}
One step each, stacked into a pipeline
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**Data inputs. User parameters. One data output.**
:::

::: {.notes}
**Blocks — ~10 s**

Bridge from the toy to the tool: the same bricks, now doing the work. No explanation
needed — the labels do it.

**The restriction — ~20 s**

A Shiny module can have arbitrary inputs, arbitrary outputs, side effects, and any
communication channel you care to invent.

A block: one or more data inputs, some user parameters, exactly one data output.
That's it. That's the stud.
:::

## A block {transition="none-in slide-out"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|3|1|5-9"}
new_join_block <- function(type = "left", by = character(), ...) {
  new_block(
    server = function(id, x, y) {
      moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
        list(
          expr = reactive(
            bquote(dplyr::join(x, y, by = .(by), type = .(type)))
          )
        )
      })
    },
    ui = function(id) join_inputs(id),
    ...
  )
}
```

::: {.notes}
**The restriction, concretely — ~40 s**

Join block: `x`, `y` in; join type and join columns as parameters; one table out.

*Pseudo-code — replace with the real thing. It has to stay at about fifteen lines:
more than that and the slide overflows at this font size.*

*`code-line-numbers` walks it in three moments — data inputs (3), user parameters
(1), the one data output (5-9) — the way the 2025 deck walked the dplyr pipeline.
Reorder to match how you say it.*

*Biggest time risk in the talk. This is the only place the audience sees what
"build a block" actually means — if it doesn't feel achievable, the ask doesn't
land.*
:::

## A small vocabulary {transition="slide"}

![](img/analysis.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.takeaway}
The tailoring lives in configuration — the code carries over.

Authoring becomes assembly.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Bridge — 35 s**

Small, well-scoped units of computation with a simple, stable API. So logic lives in
general-purpose blocks; the framework handles communication and reactivity.

The tailoring lives in configuration now, so the code carries over.

A board is a small vocabulary: blocks, and the links between them. That turns
authoring into assembly — and assembly doesn't take a big model.

*"The code carries over" is the sentence connecting complication to payoff — if it
takes more than one breath, you can't afford both ends of the argument.*

*Don't name the package: blockr.ai is on the way out, blockr.assistant on the way
in. "The assistant" stays true whichever has shipped.*
:::

**Ask + close — 30 s**

The assistant assembles. Someone still has to author the parts.

Your turn: build a block — with a **coding** assistant or without, however you
prefer. *(Say "coding assistant", not "assistant" — the line before is about the
board assistant and the two blur under one word.)*

And look out for what you *don't* have to decide — that's normally the expensive
part of making something reusable.

Testimony, honestly bounded: this worked for us. YMMV. *(First cut if the beat runs
long — the look-out-for line is already testimony, in the imperative.)*

**Landing:** that's the five minutes, and there's no Q&A. There's a lot more to
show, so come find me — I'm at this one on my own, and I'd rather talk to you than
to my laptop.

*A beat before the joke and none after. Land it and stop — no thank-you that steps
on it.*
